articles.title: Why we buy: 5 thinking errors companies exploit to make you shop
articles.content:
The Queen of Christmas, Mariah Carey, has declared “It’s time!!!!”, which can only mean one thing: the holiday season is officially upon us, with all the extra spending that entails.
If past years are anything to go by, I suspect that many of my impulse purchases will spark more guilt than joy, as they gather dust in the corners of my home. So, I was extremely interested to read a copy of Influenced: The science of why we buy by Aarron Atkinson-Toal, published last week.
An assistant professor in marketing at Durham University in the UK, Atkinson-Toal has spent much of his career studying the forces that influence consumer decision-making. Like many before him, he argues that our judgements are often driven by cognitive shortcuts called heuristics that help the brain to appraise a situation without consciously deliberating over every piece of data it receives.
Advertisement
The late Nobel prizewinning psychologist Daniel Kahneman described this intuitive thinking as System 1, as opposed to the conscious, careful calculations of System 2. Leaning on System 1 can save us a lot of time and effort in the information overload of daily life. Unfortunately, this efficiency comes at the cost of accuracy and logic, since it can be easily swayed by our emotions and tends to bypass our self-control.
“It is believed that up to 95 per cent of daily decisions are made in this subconscious and reactive way,” writes Atkinson-Toal. “That is a lot of decisions being made without full awareness of actions and consequences.”
In Influenced, he sets out the many ways that marketing schemes have been designed to exploit this – and highlights some of the most important errors that may influence our shopping – and describes our feelings after we have made our purchases.
Urgency effects
In the run-up to Black Friday, we’ll see many time-limited deals that promise huge savings. When we are rushed, we are especially likely to fall into System 1 thinking, as we prioritise speed over accuracy.
Imagine you see a new phone, discounted from £1000 to £800. Under time pressure, you will be more easily swayed by your fear of regret for missing out on the bargain, since you know that you can save £200 if you buy it now. If you had more time to decide, however, you might conclude that £800 is still too much to spend for a relatively minor upgrade.
Devices like countdown timers on online retailers’ websites when you put something in your virtual cart “are attempts to make the fast decision-making process of shoppers even faster,” writes Atkinson-Toal.
Scarcity effects
To make matters worse, these limited-time offers promote the idea of scarcity, which we tend to associate with a higher value, leading us to believe that we’re getting a better deal, argues Atkinson-Toal.
In one classic experiment, Stephen Worchel, then at the University of Virginia, and his colleagues asked participants to test various goods in the lab, including a jar of cookies. The scientists found that the participants gave consistently higher ratings if there were only two cookies in the jar, compared with 10 – even though the cookies were identical in each condition. The effect was even greater if the participants were told that the cookies were running low due to high demand from other students.
When you see a “low stock alert” on a website, or an emptying shelf in a physical shop, you are primed to make a similar judgement – compelling you to buy the product.
Anchoring and adjustment
The anchoring effect was one of the first cognitive biases that Kahneman and his colleague the late Amos Tversky documented. In one study, they asked participants to spin a “wheel of fortune” containing the numbers 0 to 100 before estimating the percentage of African countries in the UN. They found that the random number chosen by the wheel of fortune “anchored” the participants’ answers: the higher the random number, the bigger their estimate.
Anchoring is prevalent in sales. If you are first recommended a high-priced product, you will be more inclined to pay more for whatever you finally choose to buy, because the luxury good has anchored your judgement of what is reasonable.
Temporal discounting and affective forecasting
Despite our amazing capacity for mental time travel, we tend to be pretty poor at estimating how decisions today will affect our feelings in the future. We prioritise immediate rewards over our future wellbeing, a habit known as temporal discounting. We also struggle to predict how we will feel about future stresses, which are known as errors in affective forecasting.
Imagine you have been putting money aside for a trip next year. When you see that advert for a new phone, you focus on the instant excitement of unwrapping the shiny new product and forget the disappointment that may arise from finding your piggy bank empty when you come to book your holiday. “It is easier to write off today’s decisions as tomorrow’s problem,” Atkinson-Toal says in the book.
Choice overload
The sheer array of options available can leave us feeling bamboozled – a phenomenon that is sometimes called choice overload. Studies show that the more offers available, the less satisfied we may feel after having made our decision. “After the rush of Black Friday, or any purchase made under time pressure, reality often kicks in about just how much has been spent on things that were not needed, fuelling a feeling of regret and likely leading to more product returns,” writes Atkinson-Toal.
All of which is certainly going to encourage me to exercise my critical thinking before I start my holiday shopping – especially when I feel rushed to make a quick choice. Simple awareness of the forces shaping our decision-making is likely to help. From my own writing on rational thinking, I know that a good rule of thumb is to actively argue with your intuitions. If you feel the impulse to buy something super expensive, give yourself enough time to list two or more reasons why it might be a bad idea. Maybe you will still conclude that you have found the ideal bargain, but at least you will have engaged some System 2 thinking to curb some of System 1’s excesses.
I’ll also be bearing in mind two reliable findings from the broader psychological literature. Spending money on experiences tends to bring greater happiness than buying physical things; and spending money on others tends to bring greater happiness than spending money on ourselves. Hosting a generous festive party, in other words, is more likely to leave me full of good cheer than any new device.
David Robson’s latest book is The Laws of Connection: 13 social strategies that will transform your life. If you have a question that you would like answered in his column, please send him a message at davidrobson.me/contact
articles.summary: As we near Black Friday, columnist David Robson explores the psychology behind our impulse to buy things – and how marketers take advantage of our brains to push us to purchase

articles.title: AI confirms a long-suspected limit on quantum computers’ advantages
articles.content:
A decades-old, vastly influential conjecture about quantum computing has finally been proven – by AI. It confirms that a whole class of mathematical problems wouldn’t be more easily solved by quantum computers.
In 1999, Scott Aaronson at the University of Texas at Austin got stuck on a question about when exactly quantum computers could excel over their conventional counterparts.
At this time, researchers knew of at least one example of a problem where the quantum approach outshone all others: Shor’s algorithm for factoring numbers. But they suspected that this hinged on the specific mathematical structure that underlies the factoring problem.
Advertisement
Aaronson wondered whether quantum computers could also win in the opposite case, when the problem contains little to no structure and lots of randomness instead. In 2011, he and Andris Ambainis at the University of Latvia formally conjectured that, in at least one case, the answer was negative – but they couldn’t prove it.
Now, David Turturean at the start-up Physical Superintelligence (PSI) and his colleagues have used Anthropic’s Fable 5.2 model to provide that proof. This eliminates a whole class of problems from the race to understand what quantum computers are best at.
“It’s a very crisp mathematical question that has consequences for quantum computing, and it has been very hard to solve, to the degree that I had given up on it my myself,” says Ambainis.
“This might be one of the [few] remaining long-standing open questions that are worth pursuing,” says Turturean.
The problem at the heart of the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture requires a computer to answer a “yes” or “no” question after being fed a huge but random string of bits, or 1s and 0s. Could a quantum computer get an answer by looking at the string significantly fewer times than a conventional computer would have to? The pair conjectured that a conventional computer could approximate the quantum computer’s performance for most strings and without having to take much longer. More simply, you could get away with not using a quantum computer at all.
Importantly, Aaronson and Ambainis translated the statement at the core of their conjecture into the language of polynomials, recasting it as a problem in a different field of pure mathematics. “We didn’t think it would catch on like it did. People who were powerhouses in their own fields and didn’t care about quantum computing got interested,” says Aaronson.
PSI’s breakthrough builds on the work of such mathematicians. Turturean says it took about four days for Fable 5.2, which wasn’t publicly available at the time, to complete the proof, improve and refine it twice, then verify the final version with the proof-checking software Lean. The PSI team then shared the proof with Guy Blanc, Jordan Docter, Carmen Strassle and Li-Yang Tan at Stanford University in California, who studied it and wrote an exposition that unravelled its key ingredients.
In a joint statement to New Scientist, they wrote that the new proof meaningfully surpasses all studies that it draws upon. “The proofs are entirely different – and substantially more difficult. Everything is also woven together in a novel way,” they wrote.
Three days after PSI made their proof of the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture public, Supartha Podder at Stony Brook University in New York and his colleagues put forward another, shorter proof of the same thesis, developed with the aid of ChatGPT 5.6 and 6. After four months of building out the framework for their proof, one part of the work by Turturean and his colleagues “supplied the missing ingredient that allowed this approach to succeed”, the researchers wrote in their paper, which was only about seven pages long.
Shachar Lovett at the University of California, San Diego, whose work was one of the key ingredients in the PSI proof, says that this exposition reveals tricks that mathematicians can now learn from and reuse. “This helps us guide our research. What I think is going to come from these AI tools is that now we can maybe ask more ambitious questions,” he says.
But Lovett is cautious about the impact this new work might have on quantum computing, as it is more mathematical than practical, he says. In Aaronson’s view, the weight of the practical implications is also unclear. “This rules out a potential direction where you could look for quantum speed-ups, but it wasn’t a plausible direction anyway,” he says. The glaring question now is where to look for new problems that quantum computers are uniquely positioned to take on.
Determining how useful different quantum computers are has been a long running challenge – now researchers appear to have the answer
“This is far from the end of quantum speedups. Instead, it informs us on what types of problems we should consider,” wrote the Stanford team. A similar problem with a shorter or less random input string, or one for which the quantum computer doesn’t give just a “yes” or “no” answer, could still benefit from the quantum approach, they wrote. This leaves tremendously many problems, including simulating industrially relevant molecules and some optimisation problems.
Aaronson says that many of the questions related to quantum information science that are best tackled with mathematics have already been answered by AI, so it is time to formulate some new ones. Matthew Pines at PSI says he and his colleagues now also want to use AI to explore new ideas, instead of just knocking down famous problems. The future will show how successful this can be. “There is some major creative leap needed. I think that’s something where AI is not good yet,” says Ambainis.
articles.summary: An AI-powered proof has rigorously shown that using quantum computers wouldn't have huge advantages for a whole class of mathematical problems, confirming a vastly influential conjecture

articles.title: A robot has assembled a structure in space for the first time
articles.content:
A robot has built a structure in space without any help of astronauts. The first-of-its-kind achievement is a step towards autonomous in-orbit manufacturing and assembly of structures such as space stations and data centres, which will be crucial if we want to develop an orbital economy.
Sergio Pellegrino at the California Institute of Technology and his team developed their robot as part of a US Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) initiative to explore new ways to build in space. Large orbiting structures in the past have either been assembled with the help of astronauts or launched pre-assembled and folded up, spring-loaded to unfold upon release from their capsules.
But unfolding doesn’t work for more complex structures, and sending astronauts to build space stations isn’t cost-effective. “We’ve been unfolding things in space, there’s been a lot of unfolding,” says Pellegrino. “The big picture is how are we going to transition from unfolding in space to building in space.”
Advertisement
The robot that he and his team built is essentially a sophisticated arm that picks up parts and clicks them together in a process similar to putting up a tent or playing with a toy construction set. The precision involved in the movements makes this more difficult than one might expect, especially because the researchers only had 18 months to take the whole project from idea to execution in orbit.
Since its March launch from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California, the robot has been working on building a radio antenna, 1.4 metres in diameter, from a set of tubes, joints and reflective nets. As it went along, images of each step were beamed back to Earth, where the researchers checked them and troubleshot any problems with an identical robot in their lab. Construction of the antenna hasn’t quite been completed and the mission ends in December, but work has proceeded far enough to prove that this is a viable approach, says Pellegrino.
Now that it has had its first test, Pellegrino hopes that other researchers and space-flight businesses get onboard to accelerate development of faster, larger assembly systems. “I think our objective should be that in the next 5 years we start doing some of this, and in 10 years, there is the beginning for a real maturing infrastructure,” he says.
Eventually, the goal is to build much larger structures, with less troubleshooting from the ground.
Taking space-based construction out of human hands could accelerate the development of businesses and science in orbit enormously, and putting together one radio antenna in space is just the beginning.
articles.summary: Autonomous in-orbit manufacturing will be key to any future space economy, and researchers have taken the first step with a robot building a radio antenna without astronaut assistance

articles.title: Economics, not climate summits, will dictate the net-zero transition
articles.content:
The stench of hypocrisy is in the air at the COP31 summit in Turkey. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he wanted to show British leadership on climate action. Meanwhile, his government just green-lit the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea, which will emit up to 36 million tonnes of carbon dioxide without noticeably reducing energy prices, and it is considering approving the Rosebank oilfield and weakening its electric vehicle mandate.
The summit’s joint hosts, Turkey and Australia, are pushing for a clean energy revolution, but this week Turkey announced two new oilfields that would help boost production 30 per cent, while promising to double natural gas production. Australia has recently approved fossil fuel projects including a “climate bomb” coal mine extension that will emit enough carbon to kill an additional 15 million Great Barrier Reef coral colonies during every bleaching event. Meanwhile, the second biggest emitter, the US, is again boycotting the annual climate summit.
While the world shaved more than 1°C off the warming trajectory after the 2015 Paris Agreement, “collective climate action has effectively stalled”, and current policies put the world on track for a catastrophic 2.7°C rise by 2100, according to Climate Action Tracker.
Advertisement
But there is one piece of good news. The Global Carbon Budget also just announced that fossil fuel emissions are expected to slightly decrease in 2026 – something that has only previously happened during the covid-19 pandemic, the 2008 financial crisis and the break-up of the Soviet Union. Granted, the 0.4 per cent decline wouldn’t have happened without the Iran war oil crisis. But the growth in cheap solar, wind and electric vehicles has offset more emissions than the spike in oil prices.
If clean tech can keep accelerating, “a sustained peak and decline in global CO2 emissions could be a few years away”, the Global Carbon Budget report said. This means that economics, not politics, is pushing the clean energy transition forward, despite the failed leadership on display at COP31.
“Policy was never the main driver,” says Auke Hoekstra at the Eindhoven University of Technology in the Netherlands. “These technologies are simply superior.”
Hoekstra is known for his graphs showing how solar panel production has repeatedly outperformed International Energy Agency expectations. Solar is now providing 10 times more energy than when the Paris Agreement was signed in 2015, making it the fastest-growing electricity source ever, followed closely by wind.
Money talks, and electricity from solar and wind costs less on average than from natural gas or coal. In the US, the top oil-producing state, Texas, where climate denier Donald Trump won a landslide, has also become the top producer of both solar and wind power. In low-income countries like Nigeria and Pakistan, rather than waiting for governments to update expensive and unreliable fossil fuel-based power grids, people are simply installing cheap Chinese solar panels on their roofs, “leapfrogging” hydrocarbon-fuelled development altogether.
The one drawback had been that solar and wind don’t generate much energy in the evening during peak demand. But cheap batteries are quickly solving that problem. Utility and home battery storage is now growing even faster than renewable power generation.
An ambitious form of climate modelling aims to pin the blame for disasters – from floods to heatwaves – on specific companies. Is this the tool we need to effectively prosecute the world’s biggest carbon emitters?
Of course, early subsidies and regulations by governments like China and Germany created the market conditions for renewables to start coming down the cost curve. While economics is driving the energy transition, policy can speed it up or, as in the case of Trump cancelling electric vehicle subsidies, slow it down. Governments still provide more than $900 billion of annual support for fossil fuels.
The target proposed at COP31 of increasing energy use from electricity to 35 per cent by 2035 would send a positive signal. The biggest bottleneck to this is expanding the grid, something governments could accelerate at home by cutting red tape and offering subsidies and loans.
Kingsmill Bond at think tank Ember Energy thinks the economics of clean tech will let the world limit warming to much less than the projected 2.7°C by 2100. Exactly how much less depends on politics. He proposes that energy-importing countries start their own COP, where fossil fuel-exporting countries can’t delay progress.
“The old system is just being propped up by legacy policy and ignorance,” he says. “We’ve just got to tear that down.”

articles.title: Pink noise played during sleep shows promise for Alzheimer’s memory loss
articles.content:
Brief bursts of ‘pink noise’ played while people with early-stage Alzheimer’s disease sleep might give them a slight memory boost, a small study suggests.
Pink noise is best described as a low-pitched hiss. There is some evidence that exposure to pink noise during sleep may help clear waste products from the brain. As such, researchers are beginning to assess whether pink-noise therapy has benefits for the treatment of Alzheimer’s disease.
An international team of researchers has explored this possibility. They worked with 37 people, each with diagnosed with Alzheimer’s and experiencing mild cognitive impairment affecting memory. On two occasions, 14 days apart, the 37 participants were invited into the lab in the evening and asked to memorise 30 word pairs. They then slept in the lab while the researchers monitored their brain activity.
Advertisement
Javier Mínguez at Elevvo Therapeutics in Spain, and a member of the research team, says slow brainwaves and brief bursts of neural activity known as sleep spindles help the brain consolidate memories, a process Alzheimer’s can disrupt. The researchers used a system developed by Spanish neurotechnology company Bitbrain that can identify when slow brainwaves are approaching their peak. Throughout the first night in the lab, the researchers played a 50-millisecond-long pulse of pink noise to the sleeping participants each time these peaks occurred.
“Timing is critical, because the useful window is only about 200 milliseconds wide,” says Mínguez.
On the second night in the lab, the study participants were not exposed to pink noise as they slept.
After both nights, the participants were asked to recall the word pairs they had learned the evening before. They remembered slightly more word pairs after exposure to pink noise than after the night without pink noise: 0.88 word pairs more, on average, after the pink-noise exposure. This is equivalent to about a 19 per cent improvement in memory, the researchers say. The clinical significance of this result remains uncertain.
“These results are meaningful theoretically and fit with an increasingly strong set of findings linking memory storage with overnight brain activity,” says Ken Paller at Northwestern University in Illinois, who wasn’t involved in the study.
The study hasn’t yet been peer-reviewed. Several authors have commercial connections to Bitbrain or its spin-off Elevvo Therapeutics, and three are inventors on a pending patent covering the method, says Mínguez.
Mínguez sees the study as a proof of concept. To find out whether the benefits can last, the researchers are now expanding their experiments. They have given study participants equipment to use at home that offers pink noise stimulation during sleep, and they will assess the effects of continued exposure over a 6-month period.
articles.summary: There is some evidence that pink noise signals can boost the brain's ability to clear out waste products. Now there are some indications that this might improve memory performance in people with Alzheimer's
